newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi rebels report fierce fighting.
newsitem.headline: Burundi rebels report fierce fighting.

text.p: Burundi's main Hutu rebel group said on Sunday its forces were engaging army positions in five main regions of the central African nation and fierce fighting was sending thousands of refugees streaming into Tanzania.

Innocent Nimpagaritse, East Africa representative for the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), said fighting was raging in the provinces of Kayanza, rural Bujumbura, Bururi, Rutana and Ruyigi.
"As I speak to you our forces are engaging government troops in fierce battles...," Nimpagaritse said.

Nimpagaritse said the latest fighting was a major show of force by the CNDD to prove that its forces were deeply entrenched inside Burundi despite claims by Bujumbura that they had been routed from bases in eastern Zaire.
Earlier this week the Burundi army reported fighting just 15 km (eight miles) south of the capital Bujumbura.
The three-year-old civil war pits Burundi's Tutsi-led military junta against rebels drawn from the majority Hutu tribe.
"It is a massive show of force. It is a deliberate and well-calculated military campaign to prove to all that we are alive, active and firmly in control of the main provinces," Nimpagaritse added.

Regional analysts were taken aback by the latest campaign by CNDD's military wing -- Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD) -- which came six weeks after FDD forces were dislodged from bases in refugee camps in eastern Zaire.

Burundian rebels fled the eastern Zairean city of Uvira along with 225,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees because of fighting between Rwandan-backed ethnic Banyamulenge Tutsis who now control much of eastern Zaire and Zaire's ragged army.
The demise of the Zaire bases gave the Burundian army a decisive short term advantage over the rebels, who suffered substantial losses in both men and equipment, diplomats say.
Burundi military strongman Pierre Buyoya says the FDD has set up new bases in western Tanzania but Tanzania has strongly dismissed the accusation as short-sighted propaganda.

Over 150,000 people, mainly civilians who include a president and Catholic archbishop, have died in three years of civil war in the tea and coffee-growing country, but there are no casualty figures for the latest round of fighting.
Nimpagaritse said the FDD strategy was to "bombard Buyoya and his junta into direct negotiations."
Buyoya seized power in a bloodless military coup on July 25 after deposing Hutu civilian president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, who remains holed-up in the U.S. ambassador's residence in Bujumbura.

Regional states including Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda which imposed economic and transport sanctions after the coup are demanding the start of unconditional negotiations between the government and rebels before the blockade is lifted.

The latest fighting came a day after a U.N. agency warned the war in Burundi, which analysts fear could throw Burundi on the path of Rwanda where a million people were slaughtered in the 1994 genocide, was spreading rapidly and causing the widespread displacement of people and food shortages.

"The conflict in Burundi, which has been somewhat overshadowed by the problems in eastern Zaire, is spreading rapidly and causing massive population displacements," the World Food Programme (WFP) said in a statement issued in Nairobi.
WFP said clashes between rebels and government forces have displaced tens of thousands of Burundians and 80,000 of them, twice as many as a few weeks ago, are now receiving food aid.
